content: Sassafras albidum, commonly known as Sassafras, White Sassafras, Red Sassafras, or Silky Sassafras, is a deciduous tree species native to eastern North America. Its range extends from southern Maine and southern Ontario westward to Iowa and southward to central Florida and eastern Texas. It thrives in the eastern deciduous forest habitat, growing at altitudes from sea level up to 1,500 meters. Historically, it was also found in southern Wisconsin, but it is now extinct there as a native species. This tree is medium-sized, reaching heights of 15 to 35 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 60 centimeters. Its crown is composed of numerous slender branches. The bark of mature trees is thick, dark red-brown, and deeply furrowed. The branching pattern is sympodial. Young shoots are bright yellow-green with mucilaginous bark, later turning reddish-brown and developing shallow fissures within two to three years. The leaves are alternate, green to yellow-green, ovate or obovate, measuring 10–16 cm in length and 5–10 cm in width, with short, slender, slightly grooved petioles. They exhibit three distinct shapes: three-lobed leaves, unlobed elliptical leaves, and two-lobed leaves, all of which can appear on the same branch. Rarely, leaves with more than three lobes are observed. In autumn, the foliage turns yellow with red tinges. The flowers are produced in loose, drooping racemes up to 5 cm long in early spring, just before the leaves emerge. These flowers are yellow to greenish-yellow and have five or six tepals. Sassafras is typically dioecious, with male and female flowers on separate trees. Male flowers have nine stamens, while female flowers possess six staminodes (aborted stamens) and a 2–3 mm style on a superior ovary. Pollination is insect-mediated. The fruit is a dark blue-black drupe, approximately 1 cm long, containing a single seed. It is borne on a red, fleshy, club-shaped pedicel about 2 cm long and ripens in late summer. Birds are responsible for seed dispersal. The cotyledons are thick and fleshy. All parts of the plant are aromatic and spicy. The roots are thick and fleshy, often producing root sprouts that can develop into new trees. Sassafras prefers rich, well-drained sandy loam with a pH of 6–7 but can grow in any loose, moist soil. While seedlings tolerate shade, saplings and mature trees require full sunlight for optimal growth. In forests, it typically regenerates in gaps created by windblown trees. Root sprouts frequently form dense thickets, and a single tree, if left unchecked, can create a large clonal colony through its stoloniferous roots, which extend in all directions and produce numerous shoots. Sassafras is often cultivated as an ornamental tree due to its unique leaves and aromatic scent. Outside its native range, it is occasionally grown in Europe and other regions. The wood of Sassafras is dull orange-brown, hard, and durable when in contact with soil. Historically, it was used for posts, rails, small boats, and ox-yokes, though its scarcity and small size limit its current use. Some of the wood is still used for furniture making. An essential oil, known as sassafras oil, is distilled from the root bark or fruit. It has been used as a fragrance in perfumes and soaps, as well as a flavoring agent in foods such as sassafras tea and candy. It has also been employed in aromatherapy. The scent of sassafras oil is said to be an effective mosquito and insect repellent, making it a desirable garden plant. Acids extracted from the bark are used in perfume manufacturing. Historically, the oil was used as a painkiller and antiseptic in dentistry and to soothe eye inflammation and ease catarrh. Sassafras oil is the primary source of safrole, which constitutes 75–80% of the essential oil. The root or root bark has been used to make tea, although commercial sassafras teas are now artificially flavored due to an FDA ban. A yellow dye can be obtained from the wood. The shoots were once used to make root beer, which originally was an alcoholic beverage but is now a soft drink. The characteristic odor of root beer was derived from sassafras extract, which has since been replaced by other natural or artificial flavors. The dried and ground leaves are known as filé powder, which is still used as a thickening agent in sauces and soups in Cajun, Creole, and other Louisiana cuisines, most notably in the dish filé gumbo. Safrole is now recognized by the United States Department of Agriculture as a potential carcinogen. As a result, safrole and sassafras not certified as safrole-free have been banned in the United States as food additives or flavoring agents by the FDA since 1976. However, sassafras leaves do not contain sufficient amounts of safrole to fall under the FDA ban. Safrole is commonly used in clandestine laboratories to synthesize hallucinogenic drugs such as MDA (3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine), MDMA (Ecstasy), and MDEA (Love). In some rural areas, sassafras was a popular additive to moonshine and may still be used for this purpose. The name Sassafras was applied by the botanist Nicolas Monardes in the sixteenth century and is believed to be a corruption of the Spanish word for saxifrage. Before the twentieth century, Sassafras was highly regarded in medical literature but eventually became valued primarily for its ability to enhance the flavor of other medicines.
